title: U.S.-Africa Trade at a Crossroads: A Moment for New Thinking
gist: AGOA's 2028 extension is treated as an opening, not a solution: China-Africa trade ($348B in 2025) now runs more than triple US-Africa trade ($104.9B), and the authors argue Washington must move beyond tariff-preference thinking toward a broader investment/capital framework as Africa pursues its own continental integration (AfCFTA) regardless of US engagement.

themes.theme: The US-China trade gap has become structural

insights.claim: China-Africa trade reached a record $348 billion in 2025, more than three times the roughly $104.9 billion in US-Africa trade, and the gap is widening: the US began the century with a commanding trade advantage over China on the continent and now trades with Africa at a third of Beijing's volume.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The scale of the US-China Africa trade gap suggests AGOA-style incremental tariff-preference tweaks cannot close it; investors should expect continued Chinese commercial dominance across African markets absent a much larger US capital commitment.

insights.claim: US-sub-Saharan Africa trade (the actual AGOA-eligible universe) is roughly equal in size to China's trade with South Africa alone, meaning the headline US-Africa trade comparison actually understates the scale of Chinese commercial dominance on a like-for-like sub-Saharan basis.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This reframing shows the true competitive gap is even starker than the headline continental figures suggest, reinforcing that AGOA alone is not commensurate with the scale of Chinese engagement.

insights.claim: Chinese vendors Huawei and ZTE are commonly cited as having built an estimated half of Africa's 3G and approximately 70 percent of its 4G networks, and Chinese AI models are emerging as local favorites due to ease of use, low cost, and accessibility, with Chinese companies reportedly offering free computing to African companies and governments.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese digital-infrastructure and AI dominance in Africa is a durable structural lock-in that Western tech and telecom firms will find very difficult to displace without matching low-cost, high-volume offers.

insights.claim: On critical minerals, Chinese companies control the supply chain and global processing capacity for rare earths even though they directly own or operate only a small percentage of African mines, showing Chinese leverage is concentrated in midstream processing rather than upstream extraction.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western minerals strategy focused only on securing African mine equity misses the real leverage point — midstream processing capacity — which is where actual pricing power sits.

insights.claim: AGOA was never designed to compete with Chinese trade — it was intended to support sub-Saharan African market access and integration into global markets — and while it supported real manufacturing growth in Kenya, Madagascar, and Lesotho, those gains were limited to specific sectors and countries rather than economy-wide transformation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect AGOA renewal alone to catalyze broad-based African industrialization; gains will likely remain concentrated in the same narrow set of textile/manufacturing niches as before.

insights.claim: AGOA treats Africa as a collection of individual sub-Saharan markets rather than as an increasingly integrated continental bloc, even as Africa has moved toward deeper integration since 2000 through regional economic communities and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AGOA's country-by-country architecture is increasingly mismatched with how Africa itself is organizing trade, meaning US policy risks becoming structurally obsolete relative to AfCFTA-driven regional integration.

themes.theme: Africa is building its own trade architecture regardless of US action

insights.claim: Intra-African trade increased to over $192 billion in 2023, and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is being built explicitly to reduce dependence on foreign currencies, reduce payment friction, and increase intra-African trade — yet intra-African trade still represents only 15 to 18 percent of the continent's total trade.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Pan-African Payment System is a concrete de-dollarization-adjacent infrastructure project to monitor; its growth trajectory will signal how fast Africa reduces dependence on Western financial rails.

insights.claim: African leaders and economists increasingly frame their long-term interest as building resilient, local economic systems requiring increased access to capital and diversified investment — reflected in efforts like the African Credit Rating Agency, established by the African Union, aimed at reforming credit rating processes to secure more affordable credit.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A homegrown African Credit Rating Agency could eventually compete with Moody's/S&P/Fitch sovereign ratings on the continent — worth watching as a long-term shift in how African sovereign debt risk gets priced.

insights.claim: African governments are not waiting for the outcome of AGOA's modernization to determine their trade strategy; they are pursuing continental integration, diversified partnerships, and alternative payment systems regardless of the United States' ultimate level of engagement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US policymakers and investors should treat African economic diversification and de-risking from US dependency as a baseline trend, not a contingent response to US trade policy choices.

themes.theme: Structural realities demanding a new US framework

insights.claim: By 2050 Africa's working-age population will exceed 1.1 billion, the largest expansion of any labor market in the world, and sub-Saharan Africa alone will need to create an estimated 15 million jobs annually by 2030 just to absorb new entrants — a scale categorically different from what AGOA's manufacturing provisions have generated.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The scale of Africa's coming labor force growth (15M jobs/year needed by 2030) implies enormous long-term demand for light manufacturing, services, and digital-economy investment — a demographic tailwind independent of any single trade policy outcome.

insights.claim: A significant structural bottleneck limiting Africa's ability to convert market-access opportunities into competitive exports is capital, not just tariffs — AGOA was a market-access tool, not a finance instrument, and existing US instruments (DFC, MCC, EXIM, USTDA) have been deployed to Africa at a scale modest relative to the opportunity and to Chinese competition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on US-Africa trade growth is capital deployment scale from DFC/MCC/EXIM/USTDA, not additional tariff preferences — a key allocation signal for where US policy effort should concentrate.

insights.claim: A serious business access agenda for Africa requires a holistic approach beyond duty-free tariff access, including investment facilitation, standards harmonization support, insurance and loan guarantees, and bilateral regulatory engagement — frictions that trade preferences alone do not eliminate.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Firms seeking to trade with Africa face non-tariff frictions (standards, finance, regulatory mismatch) that persist even where AGOA duty-free access already applies — a reminder that market access alone doesn't guarantee trade flow.
